<section class="hero-shell" aria-labelledby="home-title">
  <div class="hero-grid">
    <div class="hero-copy">
      <p class="eyebrow">Simon Fraser University · School of Resource and Environmental Management</p>
      <h1 id="home-title">Cities <span>&</span> Climate<br>Learning Lab</h1>
      <p class="hero-tagline">How cities find, generate and use evidence for climate action.</p>
      <p class="hero-proposition">Cities learn from one another. The hard part is knowing what can travel.</p>
      <p class="hero-subtitle">No city can investigate every climate problem for itself. But a policy that worked elsewhere may depend on institutions, infrastructure or resources that are absent locally. Another study may fill a gap without changing a decision. The same intervention may produce different results depending on who delivers it and who bears its costs.</p>
      <p class="hero-lab-statement">The Cities and Climate Learning Lab studies these connections: what cities can learn from existing evidence, where new evidence would make a difference, how action is organised, and what it changes for people and places.</p>

      <p>Four connected questions.</p>

  </div>
</section>

```{=html}
<section class="section-shell intro-band" aria-labelledby="problem-heading">
  <p class="eyebrow">The urban climate learning problem</p>
  <div class="split-heading">
    <h2 id="problem-heading">Four questions decide whether evidence can help.</h2>
    <div><p>First, cities have to judge whether evidence from somewhere else fits their circumstances. They also have to decide whether new research would change anything, who can carry a policy through, and what happens to different people once it is in place.</p><p>Treating those questions separately can make a lesson look more portable, a research gap more urgent, a policy easier to deliver or a benefit more widely shared than it really is.</p></div>
  </div>
  <p class="small-note">Urban climate evidence does not become useful merely because it exists.</p>
</section>
```
